# The Heat Is Urban: How Cities Can Make Summer More Bearable

When a heat wave strikes, the temperature a person actually experiences depends less on the weather forecast than on where, exactly, that person is standing. A shaded street lined with mature trees can be fifteen degrees cooler than a sun-blasted parking lot a few blocks away. A modern apartment with good insulation and air conditioning offers refuge; a top-floor unit in a poorly sealed building can become lethal. This variation is not accidental. It is the product of decades of decisions about street design, housing policy, land use, and infrastructure—decisions that cities can revisit. As climate change makes extreme heat more frequent and more severe, making summer bearable is no longer a matter of comfort. It is a matter of public health, and it is one of the most tractable problems cities face.

## The Original Air Conditioner: Trees

The most powerful tool for cooling a city is also the oldest and cheapest: shade. Trees cool urban environments in two ways. Their canopies intercept solar radiation before it strikes pavement, and their leaves release water vapor through transpiration, which absorbs heat from the surrounding air.
